q: How do rays of light travel in a homogeneous medium? (JAC 2021, 2022)
e: Light travels along straight-line paths in a uniform medium, evidenced by sharp shadows of opaque objects.

q: What is the speed of light in vacuum? (JAC 2021, 2022)
e: Light travels fastest in vacuum with a speed c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

q: How many laws of reflection are there? (JAC 2022)
e: There are two laws of reflection: (i) ∠i = ∠r, and (ii) incident ray, normal and reflected ray all lie in the same plane.

q: What is the relation between focal length (f) and radius of curvature (R) of a spherical mirror? (JAC 2021, 2022)
e: For spherical mirrors of small aperture, the radius of curvature equals twice the focal length (f = R/2).

q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles? (JAC 2020, 2022)
e: Convex mirrors always give an erect, diminished image and curve outwards to provide a much wider field of view.

q: Which mirror is used as a shaving mirror and by dentists to see enlarged images of teeth? (JAC 2022)
e: A concave mirror forms an erect and enlarged image when the object is held within its focal length (between P and F).

q: Which mirror is used in torches, search-lights and vehicle headlights to obtain a strong parallel beam of light? (JAC 2022)
e: Placing the bulb at the principal focus of a concave mirror produces a powerful parallel beam upon reflection.

q: Which mirror is best suited for solar cookers and solar furnaces to concentrate sunlight? (JAC 2022)
e: A large concave mirror converges parallel sun rays to its focus to generate intense heat.

q: What is the nature of the image formed by a plane mirror? (JAC 2022)
o: Virtual, erect and of the same size as the object (laterally inverted)
e: A plane mirror always forms a virtual, erect, laterally inverted image of the exact same size as the object at equal distance behind it.

q: What is the focal length of a plane mirror? (JAC 2024)
e: A plane mirror is effectively a spherical mirror of infinite radius of curvature, so its focal length is infinite (∞).

q: If the radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 20 cm, what is its focal length? (JAC 2022)
e: Using f = R / 2, we get f = 20 / 2 = 10 cm.

q: Which one of the following materials CANNOT be used to make a lens? (NCERT / JAC 2022)
e: A lens must be transparent so light can refract through it; clay is opaque and cannot form a lens.

q: What is the SI unit of power of a lens? (JAC 2022)
e: The SI unit of power of a lens is dioptre (D), equal to m⁻¹.

q: What is the power of a convex lens of focal length 1 m? (JAC 2022)
e: For a convex lens f = +1 m, so P = 1 / (+1) = +1 D.

q: According to the New Cartesian Sign Convention, which lens always has a POSITIVE focal length? (JAC 2022)
e: A convex lens has a positive focal length (+f), while a concave lens has a negative focal length (-f).

q: What type of image is ALWAYS formed by a concave lens for any real object? (JAC 2022)
e: A concave lens always diverges light, producing a virtual, erect and diminished image for all positions of a real object.

q: What is the correct formula for magnification (m) produced by a spherical lens? (JAC 2022)
e: For a lens, magnification m = v/u (positive sign), whereas for a mirror m = -v/u.

q: If the power of a lens is -4.0 D, find its focal length and nature of lens: (JAC 2022, 2024, 2026)
e: f = 1/P = 1/(-4) = -0.25 m = -25 cm. Negative focal length/power indicates a concave lens.

q: How many laws of refraction are there? (JAC 2022)
e: There are two laws of refraction: coplanarity of incident ray, refracted ray and normal, and Snell's law (sin i / sin r = constant).

q: A coin placed at the bottom of a water-filled bucket appears slightly raised due to: (JAC 2022)
e: Rays emerging from denser water into rarer air bend away from the normal by refraction, raising the apparent depth.

q: What is the absolute refractive index of diamond (highest among common natural media in NCERT)?
e: According to NCERT Table 10.3, diamond has the highest refractive index of 2.42 (water 1.33, crown glass 1.52).

q: When an object is placed at the centre of curvature C of a concave mirror, where is the image formed and what is its nature? (JAC 2022, 2024)
o: At C itself, real, inverted and of the same size
e: An object at C of a concave mirror produces a real, inverted, same-sized image right at C.

q: A ray of light passing through which point of a thin lens emerges undeviated? (JAC 2022)
e: Any light ray passing through the optical centre (O) of a thin lens goes straight without any deviation.

q: Where is a point-sized image formed for an object at infinity in concave mirror, convex mirror, concave lens AND convex lens? (JAC 2025)
o: All four—concave mirror, convex mirror, concave lens and convex lens (at their respective focus)
e: For an object at infinity, all four spherical mirrors and lenses form a highly diminished, point-sized image at the focus.

q: Among air, water, glass and kerosene/oil, in which medium is the speed of light fastest? (JAC 2022, 2024)
e: Light speed v = c/n is highest in the medium with lowest refractive index—air (n ≈ 1.0003).

q: Which equation correctly represents the spherical mirror formula?
e: The mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, whereas the lens formula has a minus sign: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.

q: Which equation correctly represents the thin lens formula?
e: The thin lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f using the New Cartesian sign convention.

q: If the angle of incidence on a mirror is 60°, what is the angle of reflection? (JAC 2022)
e: By the first law of reflection, angle of reflection r = angle of incidence i = 60°.

q: What is the centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror called?
e: The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is a point called the pole (P).

q: When light travels from one medium into another during refraction, which quantity remains UNCHANGED? (JAC 2022)
e: During refraction, speed and wavelength change, whereas frequency (fixed by the light source) remains unchanged.

q: A spherical mirror and a thin spherical lens each have a focal length of -15 cm. The mirror and lens are likely to be: (NCERT / JAC 2022)
e: By the New Cartesian sign convention, both concave mirror and concave lens have negative focal lengths.

q: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get a real image of the exact same size as the object? (NCERT)
e: When an object is placed at 2F₁ in front of a convex lens, a real, inverted image of identical size forms at 2F₂.

q: Which lens would you prefer to use while reading small letters found in a dictionary? (NCERT)
o: A convex lens of focal length 50 cm
A concave lens of focal length 50 cm
A convex lens of focal length 5 cm
A concave lens of focal length 5 cm
e: A magnifying glass is a convex lens, and shorter focal length (5 cm, +20 D) provides much higher angular magnification.

q: If the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 90°, what is the angle of reflection? (JAC 2022)
e: Since ∠i + ∠r = 90° and ∠i = ∠r, we have 2r = 90°, so angle of reflection r = 45°.

q: When does a convex lens form a virtual, erect and magnified image of an object? (JAC 2022)
o: When object lies between optical centre O and focus F₁
e: When an object is within the focus (between O and F₁), a convex lens acts as a magnifying glass forming a virtual, erect, enlarged image on the same side.

q: What is the physical meaning of the statement: 'The refractive index of diamond is 2.42'? (NCERT)
o: Light travels 2.42 times faster in diamond
The ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed of light in diamond is 2.42 (so speed inside diamond drops by a factor of 2.42)
e: n = c/v = 2.42 means the ratio of light's speed in vacuum to its speed in diamond is 2.42 (light slows down to c/2.42).

q: When a light ray travels obliquely from an optically rarer medium (air) into a denser medium (glass), how does it bend?
e: Entering a denser medium slows light down, bending the ray towards the normal (r < i).

q: When a light ray passes obliquely from a denser medium (water/glass) into a rarer medium (air), how does it bend?
e: Entering a rarer medium increases light speed, bending the ray away from the normal (r > i).

q: What does a negative sign (-) in the value of magnification 'm' indicate?
e: A negative magnification indicates an inverted (and real) image below the principal axis.

q: What is the meaning of magnification produced by a plane mirror being +1? (NCERT)
o: Image size equals object size (|m|=1), and the '+' sign shows the image is virtual and erect
e: |m| = 1 means image height equals object height, while '+' denotes an erect (virtual) image.

q: Rays parallel to the principal axis after reflection from a concave mirror always pass through: (JAC 2022)
e: Any ray parallel to the principal axis passes through (concave) or appears to diverge from (convex) the principal focus F after reflection.

q: When light passes through a rectangular glass slab with parallel opposite faces, how is the emergent ray oriented relative to the incident ray?
o: Emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray direction, with a small lateral shift
e: Bending at the two parallel air–glass and glass–air interfaces is equal and opposite, keeping the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray.

q: No matter how far you stand from a mirror, your image appears erect. The mirror is likely to be: (NCERT)
e: Both a plane mirror and a convex mirror always form an erect (virtual) image regardless of object distance.

q: Which spherical mirror can form an enlarged, virtual and erect image of a close object?
o: Concave mirror (object between P and F)
e: Only a concave mirror forms a magnified virtual image (when u < f); plane gives same size and convex gives diminished.

q: What is the power of a convex lens of focal length 50 cm? (JAC 2022)
If the power of a lens is +2 D, its focal length will be: (JAC 2022)
When an object is placed beyond C of a concave mirror, where is the image formed and what is its nature?
o: Between F and C, real, inverted and diminished
e: For an object beyond C, a concave mirror forms a diminished, real and inverted image between F and C.

q: According to the New Cartesian sign convention, object distance (u) for a real object placed in front of a mirror or lens is always:
e: Since a real object is placed to the left of the mirror/lens (opposite to incident light direction), u is always negative.

q: Which mirror can easily give a full-length view of a tall building or distant tree in a small mirror?
e: Because a convex mirror forms a diminished erect image over a wide field of view, a small convex mirror fits a full tall building.

q: You are given kerosene (n=1.44), turpentine (n=1.47) and water (n=1.33). In which of these does light travel fastest? (NCERT)
e: Since v = c/n, light travels fastest in the medium with the lowest refractive index—water (1.33).

q: Which expression correctly represents Snell's law of refraction?
e: The ratio of sine of angle of incidence to sine of angle of refraction is constant for a given colour and pair of media.

q: A spherical lens produces magnification m = +3.0. What type of lens is this and what is the nature of image? (JAC 2022)
o: Convex lens; virtual, erect and 3 times magnified
e: Magnification m = +3 (> +1) means virtual, erect and 3× magnified, possible only with a convex lens when object is within focus.

q: Two thin lenses of powers +3.5 D and -1.5 D are placed in contact. What is the net power and nature of the combination?
e: Combined power P = P₁ + P₂ = +3.5 - 1.5 = +2.0 D (positive power acts like a converging/convex lens).

q: What is the power of a plane parallel glass slab?
e: Since a plane glass slab does not converge or diverge rays (f = ∞), its power P = 1/∞ = 0 D.

q: If the radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 54 cm, what is the magnitude of its focal length? (JAC 2022)
e: Magnitude of focal length f = R / 2 = 54 / 2 = 27 cm.

q: At what position of an object in front of a convex lens is magnification exactly m = -1?
e: At 2F₁, u = -2f and v = +2f, giving magnification m = v/u = -1 (real, inverted, equal size).

q: Why is the absolute refractive index of any material medium always greater than 1?
o: Because light has maximum speed in vacuum (c) and slows down in any medium (v < c), making n = c/v > 1
e: Since speed of light in any material medium v is always less than c in vacuum, the ratio n = c/v is always > 1.

q: What is the distance between the pole (P) and the principal focus (F) of a spherical mirror called?
e: The distance between the pole and the principal focus of a spherical mirror is called its focal length (f).

q: Why is a convex lens called a converging lens? (JAC 2022)
o: Because it converges a parallel beam of light rays onto a point (principal focus) after refraction
e: A convex lens bends parallel light rays inward to meet at its principal focus, earning the name converging lens.

q: If a ray of light strikes a glass–air boundary perpendicularly along the normal (angle of incidence i = 0°), what is the angle of refraction r?
e: By Snell's law, when i = 0°, sin r = 0 ⇒ r = 0°. A ray incident along the normal enters without bending.

A concave lens has focal length of 15 cm. At what distance should the object from the lens be placed so that it forms an image at 10 cm from the lens? Find m too. (NCERT)
An object is placed at 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 25 cm. Calculate the magnification m produced: (JAC 2026)
An object 5 cm in length is held 25 cm away from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the position and size of the image: (NCERT / JAC 2022)
A convex mirror used for rear-view on an automobile has a radius of curvature of 3.00 m. If a bus is located at 5.00 m from this mirror, find the image position v: (NCERT Ex 10.1)
Light enters from air to glass having refractive index 1.50. What is the speed of light in the glass? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s) (NCERT)
e: Using n = c / v, speed in glass v = (3 × 10⁸) / 1.50 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

q: A 4 cm high object is placed 30 cm from a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the height of the image formed: (JAC 2020)
A concave mirror produces three times magnified (enlarged) real image of an object placed at 10 cm in front of it. Where is the image located? (NCERT)
o: 30 cm in front of the mirror (v = -30 cm)
e: Real image means inverted, so m = -3. With u = -10 cm: -3 = -v/(-10) ⇒ v = -30 cm (30 cm in front of the mirror).

q: An object is placed at a distance of 10 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position and nature of the image: (NCERT)
o: v = +6 cm (behind the mirror), virtual and erect
e: Convex mirror: f = +15, u = -10. 1/v = 1/15 + 1/10 = 1/6 ⇒ v = +6 cm behind the mirror (virtual and erect).

q: A doctor prescribes a corrective lens of power +1.5 D. Find the focal length and nature of the lens: (NCERT)
e: f = 1/1.5 = +2/3 m ≈ +66.7 cm. Positive power denotes a converging (convex) lens.

q: Find the focal length of a convex mirror whose radius of curvature is 32 cm: (NCERT)
e: For a convex mirror, R = +32 cm, so f = R/2 = +16 cm.

q: A 2.0 cm tall object is placed perpendicular to the principal axis of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Distance of object is 15 cm. Find image distance v and magnification m: (NCERT Ex 10.4)
An object of size 7.0 cm is placed at 27 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 18 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed to get a sharp image? (NCERT Ex)
o: 54 cm in front of the mirror (v = -54 cm, h' = -14 cm)

q: The speed of light in vacuum is 3 × 10⁸ m/s and in water is 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the refractive index of water:
The refractive index of medium A is 1.5 and that of medium B is 2.0. What is the refractive index of medium B with respect to medium A (n_BA)?
A convex lens forms a real and inverted image of a needle at 50 cm from it. If the image is equal in size to the needle, find the object distance and power of the lens: (NCERT)
e: Equal-sized real image occurs at 2F: v = +50 cm ⇒ u = -50 cm and 2f = 50 cm ⇒ f = +25 cm = 0.25 m. Power P = 1/0.25 = +4 D.

q: Find the power of a concave lens of focal length 2 m: (NCERT)
e: For a concave lens, f = -2 m, hence P = 1 / (-2) = -0.5 D.

q: As an object is moved from infinity closer to the pole (P) of a convex mirror, how do the image position and size change?
o: Moves from F to infinity and inverts
Shifts from F towards P behind the mirror, and its size increases slightly (yet remains diminished, virtual and erect)
e: At infinity the image is a point at F; bringing the object closer shifts the image from F toward P between P and F, remaining virtual, erect and diminished.

q: One-half (upper half) of a convex lens is covered with black paper. A lighted candle is placed at 30 cm in front of this lens (f = 20 cm). Will this lens produce a complete image of the candle? (NCERT)
o: A complete full image of the candle is formed, though with reduced brightness (intensity)
e: Every point of the candle sends rays through the uncovered half of the lens to focus on the screen, forming a complete image of reduced brightness.

q: A ray travels from air into a transparent medium with angle of incidence i = 45° and angle of refraction r = 30°. Calculate the refractive index of the medium:
Lens A has focal length +40 cm and Lens B has focal length -20 cm. What are their respective powers?
A student stands 3 m in front of a plane mirror and then walks 1 m closer towards the mirror. What is the new distance between the student and her image?
e: New object distance = 2 m, so image forms 2 m behind the mirror. Total distance between student and image = 2 + 2 = 4 m.

q: A concave mirror has a focal length of 12 cm. At what distance from the mirror must an object be placed so that its real image is of the exact same size?
e: Same-sized real image forms at the centre of curvature C: distance R = 2f = 2 × 12 = 24 cm.

q: Given refractive indices: Ice (1.31), Water (1.33), Crown Glass (1.52), Diamond (2.42). In which medium does light travel SLOWEST?
e: Higher refractive index means slower light (v = c/n); diamond (2.42) slows light down the most.

q: When an object is placed between F₁ and 2F₁ in front of a convex lens, where is the image formed and what is its nature?
e: Placing an object between F₁ and 2F₁ forms a real, inverted, magnified image beyond 2F₂.

q: Which magnification value confirms that the mirror used is a convex mirror?
e: Only a convex mirror (among mirrors) has positive magnification less than 1 (0 < m < +1, such as +0.4).

q: Sun's rays focused by a concave mirror burn a piece of paper kept 18 cm from the mirror pole. What is the radius of curvature of this mirror?
e: Parallel sun rays converge at focus F, so |f| = 18 cm and radius of curvature R = 2f = 36 cm.

q: A lens produces a magnification of -0.5 for a 6 cm tall object. Find the height and nature of the image:
o: -3 cm, real, inverted & half the size
e: h' = m × h = (-0.5) × 6 = -3 cm; the minus sign shows the image is real and inverted.

q: If an object is placed at 20 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length +20 cm, where will the image form?
e: Since u = -20 cm = -f, the object is right at F₁: 1/v = 1/20 - 1/20 = 0 ⇒ v = infinity.

q: The refractive index of benzene is 1.50. By what percentage is the speed of light reduced when it enters benzene from air?
e: Speed in benzene v = c/1.5 = (2/3)c. Reduction = (1/3)c = 33.3%.

q: Case Study: A student focuses sunlight onto a sharp spot 12.0 cm from a concave mirror. Then she places a candle 15.0 cm in front of the same mirror. Where is the candle's image formed?
o: 60 cm in front of the mirror (v = -60 cm), real, inverted and 4× enlarged

q: Case Study: Light travels at 2.4×10⁸ m/s in X, 2.0×10⁸ m/s in Y, and 1.5×10⁸ m/s in Z. A ray goes obliquely X → Z → Y. How does it bend at X→Z and Z→Y boundaries respectively?
o: X→Z bends towards normal (slows down); Z→Y bends away from normal (speeds up)
e: From X to Z light slows down (denser) → bends towards normal; from Z to Y it speeds up (rarer) → bends away from normal.

q: Case Study: An optician tests spectacles for Ramesh (-2.5 D) and Suresh (+2.0 D). What are the focal lengths and types of lenses in their spectacles?
o: Ramesh: +40 cm convex; Suresh: -50 cm concave
Ramesh: -40 cm concave lens; Suresh: +50 cm convex lens
e: Ramesh: f = 1/(-2.5) = -0.4 m = -40 cm (concave). Suresh: f = 1/(+2.0) = +0.5 m = +50 cm (convex).

q:
Case Study: A student recorded image distances (v) for a convex lens:
(1) u = -60 cm, v = +30 cm
(2) u = -40 cm, v = +40 cm
(3) u = -30 cm, v = +60 cm
(4) u = -10 cm, v = +30 cm
First, find f from (2). Which observation is WRONG?
o: f = +20 cm; wrong observation (4) because for u = -10 cm (< f), v must be -20 cm (virtual on same side), not +30 cm
e: Since |u|=|v|=40 cm gives 2f=40 ⇒ f=+20 cm. At u=-10 cm, 1/v = 1/20 - 1/10 = -1/20 ⇒ v = -20 cm, making '+30 cm' in (4) physically wrong!

q: Case Study: Car side-view mirrors carry the warning 'Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear'. Why do approaching cars look smaller/farther?
o: The convex mirror forms a strongly diminished image, which our brain interprets as being farther away than its actual distance
e: A convex mirror makes an erect, diminished image to capture a wide view; our eye-brain judges smaller images as farther away.

q: Case Study: Standing very close to three mirrors A, B and C: Mirror A shows the same face size; Mirror B shows a huge face; Mirror C shows a tiny face. Identify A, B and C respectively:
e: Plane mirror (A) → same size; Concave mirror within focus (B) → magnified erect; Convex mirror (C) → diminished erect.

q: Case Study: A 2.0 m deep swimming pool filled with clear water (n = 4/3) appears only 1.5 m deep when viewed nearly vertically from above. Why?
o: Refraction shifts apparent depth = real depth / n = 2.0 / (4/3) = 1.5 m
e: Rays emerging from the pool floor into air bend away from the normal, lifting the apparent depth by a factor of n (2.0 / 1.333 = 1.5 m).

q: Case Study: Two thin lenses of focal lengths +25 cm and -50 cm are kept in contact. Calculate the net power of the combination:

Assertion (A): A concave lens always forms a virtual and erect image for any real object.
Reason (R): A concave lens diverges light rays after refraction so they never actually intersect, appearing to diverge from a point on the incident side.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains A.

q:
Assertion (A): Mirror magnification m = +2 means the image is virtual, erect and twice the size of the object.
Reason (R): Mirror magnification m = +2 can only be produced by a concave mirror.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R correctly pins it down to concave mirrors (plane has m=+1, convex has 0<m<+1).

q: Case Study: A light ray hits two parallel slabs at the same angle of incidence 30°: Slab 1 is Crown Glass (n=1.52) and Slab 2 is Diamond (n=2.42). In which slab will the angle of refraction 'r' be smaller (more bending towards normal)?
o: In diamond (since sin r = sin i / n, larger n gives smaller r and stronger bending towards normal)
e: By Snell's law, sin r = sin i / n, so higher refractive index produces a smaller angle of refraction r (greater bending).

q: Case Study: A light ray hits a plane mirror along the normal (i = 0°). Keeping the incident ray fixed, the mirror is rotated by 15°. By what angle does the reflected ray rotate?
e: Rotating the mirror by θ = 15° rotates the normal by 15°, making i = 15° and r = 15°, so the reflected ray rotates by 2θ = 30°!

q:
Assertion (A): Both focal length and radius of curvature of a concave mirror are negative.
Reason (R): For a concave mirror, both F and C lie in front (to the left) of the reflecting surface.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains the negative sign convention.

q:
Assertion (A): When light enters from air into water, its speed changes while its frequency stays constant.
Reason (R): Frequency depends solely on the light source, whereas wave speed depends on the medium's refractive index.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains A.

q: Case Study: A glass convex lens (n = 1.50) has focal length 20 cm in air. If immersed completely in water (n = 1.33), what happens to its focal length and converging power?
o: Focal length increases and converging power decreases (because relative refractive index difference between glass & water is smaller than glass & air)
e: Relative refractive index drops from 1.50 (glass-air) to ~1.13 (glass-water), reducing refraction bending so focal length increases and power drops.

q: A concave mirror has focal length 20 cm. At what TWO different object distances can an object be placed so that the image formed is double the size of the object (|m| = 2)?
o: 30 cm (real image m=-2) and 10 cm (virtual image m=+2)

q: Similarly, at what TWO different object distances from a convex lens of focal length +20 cm is a double-sized image (|m| = 2) formed?
A lens gives magnification m = +1/3 when an object is placed in front of it. If the focal length magnitude is 30 cm, identify the lens and exact object distance u:
e: 0 < m < +1 is exclusively a concave lens (f = -30 cm). With v = u/3: 3/u - 1/u = -1/30 ⇒ 2/u = -1/30 ⇒ u = -60 cm.

q: A convex glass lens (n = 1.50, power +5 D in air) is completely immersed inside a clear liquid that ALSO has refractive index 1.50. How does the lens behave now?
o: Since n_lens = n_liquid = 1.50, rays suffer zero refraction at boundaries—focal length becomes infinite, power drops to 0 D, and the lens acts like a flat invisible medium
It turns into a concave lens
e: With zero refractive index contrast (1.50 / 1.50 = 1), light passes undeviated: f = ∞ and P = 0 D.

q: Given refractive index of water w.r.t. air n_w = 4/3 and glass w.r.t. air n_g = 3/2. Find (i) refractive index of water w.r.t. glass and (ii) refractive index of glass w.r.t. water respectively:
A concave mirror forms a real image on a screen placed 60 cm in front of it when an object is placed 20 cm in front of the mirror. What is the focal length and magnification?
If the lower half of a concave mirror's reflecting surface is painted black, what happens to the image of an object placed in front of it?
o: Only half of the object appears
A complete image is still formed, though with half brightness/intensity
e: Rays from all parts of the object still reflect off the upper uncovered half to form a complete image at reduced brightness.

q: A +20 cm convex lens and a -20 cm concave lens are placed tightly in contact. An object is placed 10 cm in front of this combination. Where does the final image form?
o: At the exact same object position (no net focusing, as P_net = 0 D like a flat glass plate)
e: Net power P = +5 D + (-5 D) = 0 D (f = ∞), so the combination acts like a flat glass sheet causing zero net convergence/divergence.

q: Three mirrors produce magnifications m₁ = +1, m₂ = +0.5 and m₃ = -0.5 respectively. Identify the three mirrors in order:
e: m = +1 is plane mirror; m = +0.5 (virtual diminished) is convex mirror; m = -0.5 (real inverted) is concave mirror.

q: An object and a screen are kept 40 cm apart. A convex lens placed midway between them forms a sharp, same-sized real image (m = -1) on the screen. What is the power of the lens?
e: For m = -1, object and screen are at 2f each side: total separation = 4f = 40 cm ⇒ f = +10 cm = +0.1 m. Power P = 1/0.1 = +10.0 D!

q: A ray passes from air (n=1) into water (n=4/3) and then into glass (n=3/2). What is the final speed of light inside glass compared to vacuum speed c?
e: Speed in a medium depends only on its own absolute refractive index regardless of prior layers: v_glass = c / (3/2) = (2/3)c.

q: A student wants to cast a 3 times magnified real image of a candle flame on a screen using a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. At what distance from the mirror should the candle be placed?
e: Real 3× means m = -3 ⇒ v = 3u. Mirror formula: 1/(3u) + 1/u = -1/15 ⇒ 4/(3u) = -1/15 ⇒ u = -20 cm.

q: If a symmetric convex lens of focal length f (power P) is cut vertically along the plane perpendicular to its principal axis into two identical plano-convex lenses, what becomes the focal length and power of each half?
o: Focal length becomes f/2 and power 2P
Focal length doubles to 2f and power halves to P/2
e: Since placing the two cut plano-convex halves back together restores P = P_half + P_half, each half has power P/2 and focal length 2f!

q: If the same convex lens of focal length f is cut horizontally along its principal axis into two halves, what is the focal length of each cut piece?
o: Same focal length f (unchanged, only image brightness halves)
e: Cutting along the principal axis keeps both surface curvatures unchanged, so the focal length remains f (just like covering half the lens with black paper).

q: Compare magnification m = +1 from a plane mirror and m = -1 from a concave mirror/convex lens. What is the key difference?
o: m = +1 is virtual and erect (cannot be caught on screen), whereas m = -1 is real and inverted (can be cast on screen)
e: Both produce same-size images (|m|=1), but '+' indicates virtual/erect and '-' indicates real/inverted.

q: Mirror X can only produce magnifications strictly between 0 and +1 (e.g., +0.2, +0.6), whereas Mirror Y can produce -0.5, -1, -3, and +2. Identify X and Y:
o: X = convex mirror, Y = concave mirror
e: Convex mirrors always produce diminished erect virtual images (0 < m < +1); concave mirrors span negative real magnifications and positive enlarged (>+1).

q: A runner approaches a stationary plane mirror at a speed of 4 m/s. At what relative speed does his image appear to approach HIM?
e: With respect to the mirror, the image moves at 4 m/s in the opposite direction; hence relative to the runner, the image approaches at 4 + 4 = 8 m/s.

q: Lenses of powers -2.5 D and +5.0 D are kept in contact. An object is placed 80 cm in front of the combination. Find the image position v:
e: P_net = +2.5 D ⇒ f = +40 cm. Object at 80 cm means u = -2f, so image forms at +2f = +80 cm (real, inverted, equal size).

q: When light enters a transparent medium X from air, its speed drops to half of its speed in air. What is the refractive index of medium X?
e: If speed becomes v = c/2, refractive index n = c / (c/2) = 2.0.

q: Using a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm (R = 30 cm), which pair of object distances u₁ and u₂ produces (i) a diminished real image and (ii) a magnified virtual image respectively?
o: u₁ = 40 cm (beyond C), u₂ = 10 cm (between P and F)
e: Beyond C (40 cm > 30 cm) gives a diminished real image; within F (10 cm < 15 cm) gives an enlarged virtual image.

q: A light ray enters a glass slab from air at an angle of incidence i = 60° and gets refracted at an angle r = 35°. By what angle has the ray deviated from its original straight path?
e: Going from air to glass (rarer to denser), the angle of deviation is δ = i - r = 60° - 35° = 25°.

q: A spherical mirror always produces an erect and diminished image regardless of where the object is placed in front of it. What is the sign of its focal length and radius of curvature?
o: Both positive (+) — it is a convex mirror
e: A mirror always giving an erect, diminished image is convex, for which both f and R are positive (+).

q: Can a biconvex glass lens (n = 1.5) ever behave as a diverging lens?
o: Yes, if immersed in a transparent liquid having a refractive index GREATER than glass (e.g. CS₂, n = 1.63 > 1.50)
e: When the surrounding medium has higher refractive index than the lens material (n_medium > n_lens), refraction reverses and a convex lens diverges parallel light!

q: A convex lens forms a 3× magnified virtual image (m = +3) at a distance of 30 cm on the same side as the object (v = -30 cm). Find the focal length of the lens:
Two convex lenses of focal lengths 10 cm and 40 cm are placed in contact. What is the effective focal length of the combination?
The left–right reversal seen in mirrors is called lateral inversion. Minimum how many light rays starting from an object point are usually traced to locate its image in ray diagrams?
o: At least 2 intersecting rays; lateral inversion
e: Left-right reversal is lateral inversion, and at least two reflected/refracted rays from a point are traced to locate where they intersect.

q: A light beam hits an air–glass boundary perpendicularly (i = 0°). Identify which pair CHANGES vs which pair stays UNCHANGED inside glass:
o: Speed and wavelength decrease; direction (stays along normal) and frequency remain unchanged
e: At i = 0°, direction does not bend and frequency stays fixed, yet entering denser glass slows speed (v=c/n) and shortens wavelength (λ'=λ/n).

q: Parallel rays from infinity fall on a spectacle lens of power -1.25 D. From what distance behind/in front of the lens do the emerging diverged rays appear to originate?
o: -80 cm (80 cm in front of the lens at its virtual focus)
e: f = 1/(-1.25) = -0.80 m = -80 cm. Being a diverging (concave) lens, parallel rays appear to originate from F₂ at 80 cm in front.

q: A student focuses a distant illuminated building sharply onto a wall 25 cm behind a convex lens. Why can she NOT repeat this direct projection on the wall using a concave lens?
o: Because a concave lens forms only virtual images that cannot be projected onto a screen/wall; only real images can be caught on a screen
e: Distant objects focus on the wall at f = +25 cm for a convex lens, whereas a diverging concave lens cannot produce a real image on a screen.

q: Sign convention check: For an optical mirror forming an image of a real object, we are given u < 0, v < 0, and |v| > |u|. Which deduction is 100% guaranteed?
o: It MUST be a concave mirror forming a real, inverted and magnified image (object placed between F and C)
e: In mirrors, v < 0 means real & inverted (possible only for concave mirror), and |v| > |u| gives |m| > 1 (magnified), placing the object between F and C.
